The short version

Four steps to a brief worth quoting

If you read nothing else on this page, this is the order that makes the whole thing easier.

  • Work out the servingsBefore anything else. It decides tin sizes, tiers and most of the price, and it is the number hardest to change late.
  • Name a style, or send a photographEither works. Two references and a sentence about what you like in each beats a whole album.
  • Describe the roomIndoors or out, seated or standing, and what time the cake is cut. It changes the covering and the delivery window.
  • Say what is fixedA colour, a flower, a date, a dietary requirement. Makers can work around almost anything once they know which part cannot move.

Answered

The questions people ask first

How do I describe the cake I want?

Name a style if you can, and send two or three reference images with a sentence about what you like in each. If you cannot name a style, describe the room instead: who is there, what time it is, whether it is indoors, and what the rest of the table looks like. A maker can work from that. The one thing worth avoiding is a long list of features, because a cake carrying five strong ideas usually reads as none of them.

How much cake do I actually need?

Count the people who will genuinely eat cake, then decide whether you are cutting dessert portions or the smaller wedding portions, because the same cake honestly serves very different numbers depending on which you mean. A 25cm round gives roughly 24 to 28 dessert servings or 35 to 40 wedding portions. The serving guide has the full table by tin size and tier combination.

When should I start looking?

Six to twelve months for a wedding, four to eight weeks for a milestone celebration, two to four weeks for a birthday cake, and longer again once a theme or sugar florals are involved. The limit is almost always the maker's calendar rather than the build. If your date is closer than that, ask anyway and say where you can be flexible.
